basis: US Treasury daily par yield curves (nominal CMT and real TIPS), bond-equivalent yields with semiannual compounding; tenor in years. These are par yields, not zero-coupon spot rates. Breakeven = nominal par yield minus real par yield at the same maturity on the same date.

breakeven10yBasis: Derived: Treasury 10-year nominal par yield minus 10-year TIPS par real yield on the same date. Both are par (bond-equivalent, semiannual) yields read from Treasury fitted curves, not zero-coupon rates.
notes: Curves are US Treasury par yield curves: the yield at which a hypothetical Treasury security priced at par would trade, read from Treasury's monotone convex spline fitted to bid-side prices of the most recently auctioned securities. Yields are bond-equivalent with semiannual compounding. They are par yields, not zero-coupon spot rates. Maturities under one year are shown in years (for example, 6 months = 0.5).

Every business day is shown from October 24, 2023; earlier dates back to January 2017 are thinned to the last observation of each month. Daily benchmark yields and the 10-year breakeven are kept for every business day since January 2017. Missing values are left blank, not interpolated; non-trading dates are excluded. Nominal maturities vary over time: 2-month from October 2018, 4-month from October 2022 and 1.5-month from February 2025. Before a maturity was introduced it is left blank, as in the Treasury files.

Breakevens are a dashboard calculation: nominal par yield minus TIPS real par yield at matched 5, 7, 10, 20 and 30-year maturities on matching dates only. Because both are par yields on coupon-bearing securities rather than zero-coupon rates, this is an approximation of CPI-U inflation compensation; it includes inflation risk premia and relative liquidity premia (TIPS are less liquid) and is not an inflation forecast.

The dashed overlay on the real-yield and breakeven charts is the Federal Reserve Board staff TIPS curve (Gurkaynak, Sack and Wright): par real yields and par inflation compensation for each maturity from 2 to 20 years. It is a separately fitted model, not an official Federal Reserve statistic, and is published with about a week's lag, so each chart shows its latest date on or before the selected date. Its values differ from Treasury's at matching maturities because the two curves are fitted differently.
Treasury publishes the curves each business day after market close; observation dates are not publication or retrieval dates. Treasury may revise past values.
